utterances.text: Tell me, since you completed the academy maybe you can assist us, what does it mean head of staff -- assistant to the head of staff for interventions and operational planning, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object. There's no foundation that this witness has any knowledge of this document that he assisted in the drafting of it or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac, what is your basis for asking this question of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness completed the military academy. Now he's an instructor at the school -- well, the gendarme instructor and he's a highly positioned official within the police. I'm interested in the staff for K and M. He says he's not familiar with the document; however, my question is simple: He should offer his interpretation given his educational background and given his current post to tell us what it means, assistant head for intervention and operational planning. What is operational planning?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I maintain my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll sustain the objection to this question. There is no basis so far established for this witness to have knowledge on which he could say on -- say anything that would assist us in relation to the nature of the position referred to as assistant head for interventions and operational planning of the MUP staff. If you want to pursue the matter further, you'll need to establish some foundation for doing so, Mr. Bakrac. There's nothing to suggest that this is a military document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not a military document, it's a police document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've adjudicated the matter. Please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Let us have a look at Exhibit 5D476 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document of the Pristina Corps command dated the 9th of April, 1999. Please read the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: "The staff of the Serbian MUP for Kosovo and Metohija has issued an order to all secretariats of the interior to commence planning actions to crush the terrorist groups that remain in their respective zones of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, do you know whether the MUP staff for KiM issued any orders to the secretariats to commence with such planning?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at Exhibit P1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, this is minutes of a meeting held in Pristina at the staff for K and M. It seems that among those present your commander, Bosko Buha, was there as well. We can see that on the first page. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let us go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just take the break to indicate an apparent error in translation in the English. At line 6 it says the 122nd International Brigade where as in the Serbian it just says "INT" period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Line 6 of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of this document, Your Honour, P1993. It's on the screen right now, item 6 or paragraph 6 says 122 International Brigade, whereas in the Serbian it says 122 INT period in the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, looking at number 6 on that page, would you read that line to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 6: "Deputy commander of the 122nd Intervention Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Nikolic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would note that at page 2 of both the English and B/C/S, item number 2 has INT period with a parenthetical as intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- my curiosity, Mr. Ilic, but what is the relationship in the command structure between Nikolic and Buha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragan Nikolic was Colonel Zivaljevic's deputy in the part of the 122nd Intervention Brigade that was located in the area of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, he had no direct dealings with Bosko, Commander Bosko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, let us have a look at page 6 of the document next, it's the penultimate page. Please read out -- we can see here that the assistant minister of the interior, and as you said he was also commander of the PJP, took part in a discussion. In item 1 it says: "Anti-terrorist actions." I'm interested in the next paragraph beginning with: "Now it should be organized ..." Could you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: "Smaller actions should be organized or sporadic local actions should be organized in many minor positions (places). Each SUP and OPJP," I don't know what it stands for exactly, "will establish a list of priorities in anti-terrorist actions with a detailed plan to be approved by the staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You don't know what OPJP stands for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: OPJP, I cannot recall. PJP is special police units, but I'm confused by the O. The O probably stands for "odred," detachment, detachment of the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in this record, in these minutes, from the MUP staff meeting dated the 11th of May the assistant minister and commander of the PJP clearly states, points out that every SUP and every PJP detachment shall set their own order of priorities, so they do it on their own of the anti-terrorist actions with a detailed plan that would be approved by the MUP -- by the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the planning of anti-terrorist actions for the MUPs for compositions is carried out in the SUP and the PJPs on the order issued by the assistant minister and commander of the PJP and the staff approves these plans; is that not evident?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. That's calling for speculation beyond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's calling for speculation beyond the scope of the document, beyond the scope of the knowledge that the witness has thus far given us as to any foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, what's your basis for saying that the witness would know what was happening beyond his own direct experience of his involvement in what he's already told us about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is possible that Bosko Buha, the commander, or Dragan Nikolic, I don't know now who the original commander of the witness's was, conveyed his impressions of the meeting that was held at the MUP staff, or rather, not his impressions but what General Obrad Stevanovic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if that's what you want to ask him, please ask him that; but don't ask him to interpret a document and speculate about what might have happened in relation to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did your commander, whoever it was, convey to you that Obrad Stevanovic at the meeting that was held at the MUP staff ordered that detailed, precise plans would be established by the SUPs and the PJP detachments in the fight against terrorists along with precise plans that would be approved by the staff? Was this information conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ilic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Hannis. Obviously my recollection of identity is deserting me today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ilic. You told us --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- in your background that after you completed the academy you worked as an assistant commander and then as a station commander, that is to say the commander of a police station. What police station were you a commander of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: The Grocka police station, it is a police station of the secretariat of the interior of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how big a station is that? How many men did you command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: It's a second-class police station, as far as I can recall, and it had about 120 employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from when to when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: From 1993 until 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, what would be a second-class police station? I mean, were they classified as first-class and second-class police stations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A first-class police station is a bigger police station with a larger number of employees and they probably -- and they most often belonged to cities. Belgrade has a total of 16 municipalities, ten of them are big ones, urban ones, and six are smaller ones in the rural part surrounding metropolitan Belgrade. So the smaller ones are those that have a smaller number of employees and they're called second-class police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you have been engaged in the PJP since their establishment in 1993. Does the PJP still exist today?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Special police units were disbanded when the gendarmerie was established, that is to say in 2000 or in 2001. I think it was 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that according to the rules on the use of special police units, and you said that you didn't know the exact title of the document, the tasks of the PJPs are defined, included anti-terrorist actions. Now, what do you know about who gets to decide whether, when, where, and how the PJP will be used? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I knew then as platoon commander and deputy commander of a company and ultimately commander of a company that PJPs in the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade are engaged by the chief of the police administration upon approval of the commander of the PJPs. Ex officio he always has to know about the engagement of special police units and he should approve that officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1998 and 1999, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two people there, Mr. Hannis, are there not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One's the chief of the police administration and the other is the commander of the PJP. Do you know the identity of either of these in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the commander of the special police units in 1998 and 1999 was General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you didn't know who the chief of the police administration was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and in 1999 I think that the chief of the police administration was the same person, General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the PJP in 1998 and 1999, did you hold a rank; and if so, what was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In 1998 I was a major and in 1999 I was a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you get promoted?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said earlier in your testimony that you came to Kosovo in June of 1998. Did you stay there the whole time or did you go back to Belgrade for a while and then return again later? Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: No, I was not there all the time. I came in the beginning of June 1998, that's when I came to Kosovo. On the 25th of June I returned to Belgrade. In the beginning of July of the same year I went back to Kosovo and I stayed there sometime until the beginning of September. However, a few times I would be off during the weekend. These were long weekends, five or six days that I would be off, but I don't know exactly when that was. When the agreement was signed on the reduction of forces, security forces in Kosovo - I don't know the exact name of this agreement - with half of the unit of the Belgrade detachment - at that time it was still called the detachment - but I'm talking about the unit that is the counterpart of the 122nd Brigade. So half of that unit was withdrawn from Kosovo to Belgrade to carry out their regular duties and tasks, and I went to Belgrade along with them. Sometime in the month of November, I think, I came to Kosovo yet again with a part of that unit, I think it was three or four companies. The commander of that part -- or perhaps it would be better for me to say the leader of that shift was Bosko Buha and I was his deputy, and we were stationed in Pec. In February 1999 -- well, I'm trying to say that after that shift I returned to Belgrade. And in February 1999, yet again I came to Kosovo with approximately the same forces, that is to say four companies. I was stationed in Pec and that is when I was the leader of that particular shift. I don't know exactly when it was that I returned to Belgrade, I think it was the beginning of March; and in Belgrade I carried out my regular tasks up until a day or two before the bombing started, so that would be the 22nd or 23rd of March, that's when I came to Kosovo. I came on my own and I joined Colonel Zivaljevic in part of the 122nd Intervention Brigade, in that part that was in Podujevo. I was sent there on the orders of the commanding officer of my home unit in Belgrade because our company commander got killed. So this company had a very low morale because that was a very popular commander, the one who got killed. My task was to deal with the psychological situation and the morale of the unit and to take part in action with them as company commander. During those days this action was being carried out in the area of Podujevo. I cannot remember exactly what the names of the villages were. If we were to have a map here I would remember, but it was the area of Podujevo. This action went on for about seven or eight days approximately, and after that action, at the request of Bosko Buha, that is to say the commander of that part of the detachment that was in Pec, and with the approval of Commander Zivaljevic, I was moved to Pec, or rather, the part of the detachment that was commanded by Bosko Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there because it's almost time for our break and we'll pick up afterwards if that's all right with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ilic, we need a break again at this stage for half an hour. Could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, I think you before the break told us that you had come back to Kosovo a day or two before the bombing started. After that, did you remain in Kosovo until the middle of June when the agreement was signed and the Serbian forces withdrew from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, and on a couple of occasions I had extended weekends of five to six days each.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. You told us before that the -- you think the 121st and the 122nd Detachments merged in October 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately at that time although I cannot be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when each of those were independently first formed, when was the 121st formed and when was the 122nd formed? And I'm talking about the detachments right now.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: The 122nd Detachment, I believe, was formed when the 121st and 122nd were merged, or rather, 122nd Brigade was created when the two detachments merged sometime in October 1998. As for the exact dates when the two brigades -- I mean detachments were formed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But in June 1998 when you first went to Kosovo, what unit were you a part of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: It was an ad hoc unit that was formed out of four PJP companies and the secretariat in Belgrade. The commander at the time was Dragan Nikolic. That shift lasted for 25 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did it end?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: That tour of duty was concluded towards the end of June 1998 and the unit left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then I think you told us you returned in July of 1998. Approximately when did you come back?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As part of what unit?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Again, another ad hoc unit was formed out of some other PJP companies and the secretariat in Belgrade. The head of that shift was Colonel Dragan Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's been very difficult for me to understand or follow how this works. That ad hoc group that you were in in June 1998, did it not have a name or a number?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: It is complicated. It is even difficult for me to try and remember how those shifts were formed, but that's how things went. At that time, being in Kosovo, the only way to go about it we believed was to make those short shifts rotating the various units from Belgrade. In other words, one shift was in Kosovo and the other one was, so to say, resting, performing their regular tasks at the secretariat in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I'm not sure you've answered my question yet. Did you have a name or a number for that ad hoc group you were in when you were in Kosovo in June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In June 1998 I believe we did not have a number that would designate the title of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about in July 1998 when you came back, did that ad hoc group have a name or a number?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't think it had a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were orders, written orders, directed to that ad hoc group? There must have been some way to identify you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how written orders were being sent; however, I know that we were identified as the Belgrade detachment of the PJP as opposed to other units. I truly cannot recall whether we had a number at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if you had any kind of a radio call-sign or code-name in July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I remember that call-signs changed. I remember one, though, Lazar used during the Klecka action; I, myself, was Lazar 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall now approximately when the Klecka action was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: It began in late August. It lasted for four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I wanted to ask you a question about your unit designators in 1999, and I'd like you to look at an exhibit, that's the -- it's from April of 1999 and it's Exhibit Number P1989. I may have a hard copy here I can hand you. I don't know if you've ever seen this before, you may not have, it's from a meeting of the 4th of April 1999 of senior officials in Kosovo and Metohija. And it mentions that PJP detachment commanders attended, but I don't see your name here. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go to -- I think we have to go to page 2 of the B/C/S and scroll to the bottom, and in the English same place. Did you know of a detachment commander named Radoslav Mitrovic, apparently he was commander of the 37th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally; however, at that time I had only heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the bottom of this page we see a reference to Borislav Josipovic as detachment commander for the 23rd Detachment. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received orders from him after Bosko was injured -- wounded after the Jablanica action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately when was that that Buha got wounded and was replaced by Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Bosko was wounded in early June; however, Josipovic did not replace him at the post of the Belgrade part of the detachment, I did. However, in that action -- may I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: But it was only in that action that I received orders from Borislav Josipovic. Once it was over the practice stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see listed here on this page Bosko Buha as detachment commander for the 21st Detachment and Dragan Zivaljevic detachment commander for the 22nd. Can you tell us in April of 1999 what was the connection or the nexus between these three PJP detachments, the 21st, the 22nd, and the 23rd, are all three of those members of some larger brigade; and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: The 21st and the 22nd Detachment, as stated here, is actually the 122nd Intervention Brigade; as for the 23rd Detachment, it was a separate detachment comprising personnel from various secretariats in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Apart from the 21st and 22nd Detachments then in April 1999, were there any other detachments that made up the 122nd Intervention Brigade or was that the totality of that brigade in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In April 1999 and generally speaking, both 1998 and 1999 the 122nd Detachment, or rather, intervention brigade included only the workers of the Belgrade secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that just the 21st and 22nd Detachments then or was there some other subunit of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I think there was also a territorial detachment. I cannot remember what their number was and I don't know whether they were a part of the 122nd Intervention Brigade. I think they were a separate detachment since territorial detachments were separate from manoeuvring detachments and I've been referring to manoeuvring detachments all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. During 1998, all the time that you were in Kosovo after July, were you a member of this Belgrade detachment or did you ever become a member of some other numbered detachment or did the Belgrade detachment take on a number sometime in 1998, if you follow me?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If, for example, I were trying to find you in October or November 1998, how would I ask for you, say, I'm looking for Mr. Ilic, colonel -- well, Major Ilic or Vladimir Ilic and he's with one of the PJP groups but I don't know which one, where would I look to find you if I wanted to mail you a note or something? What number would I write on it or what address? Was it still the Belgrade detachment for the whole time in 1998 or did you ever have another unit designator?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: If you mean October and November specifically, at that time I was in Belgrade at the secretariat in Belgrade performing regular tasks. That's where you would have found me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about August, September, October?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In August I was in Kosovo, in September I don't know whether I was there the whole month. Maybe I'm uncertain about the dates, but if I may assist when the agreement was signed on the reduction of the number of police forces in Kosovo, a few days later together with one half of that unit and Commander Bosko Buha I left for Belgrade. I don't know what exact date it was, but I relate that to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we know from other evidence that that agreement was around the 25th of October, 1998, so we'll say late October 1998 you left. Between July 1998 and the end of October 1998 was the unit that you were with ever known by any other designator or name than the Belgrade detachment of the PJP? Did you ever have another name or a number, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not. The unit was known as the Belgrade detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us how during -- until August or early September 1998 you used to wear the blue camouflage uniforms, but then you got your green ones and you wore those from then onwards. And you told us that the other PJP units that you participated with in 1999 wore those same uniforms. But you don't know, do you, if some of the other PJP units in Kosovo took even longer to receive their green uniforms, that is, that they may not have gotten green uniforms until sometime after September 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I think the uniforms were delivered successively and I don't know what unit got their new uniforms when. I cannot recall exactly from my unit's unit, let alone other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You described the insignia that you wore on your uniforms, you talked about the coat of arms of the PJP and the flag of Serbia. How were those patches attached to the uniforms? Were they sewn on or did you have Velcro fasteners or what, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I think we had fasteners, Velcro fasteners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned wearing the ribbons in 1998 and you mentioned how hot it was in July and August that year. Could I show you a photo, it's Exhibit P3111. You explained how it was very hot and some people actually did wear bandannas. Can you see that photograph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the people in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which one or ones, where they're standing, and who they are.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I can recognise the people standing, going from the left, Mile Novakovic; in the middle, I cannot make his face out clearly, but I think it is policeman Salipur; and the in the row below I see Goran Radosavljevic, Guri, going from the right-hand side he's the second person in the green uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see the guy on the left wearing a headband, you don't know who he is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the back row the guy on the left doesn't appear to be wearing a PJP uniform shirt, he's just wearing a T-shirt; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: You mean the person on the left -- the first person on the left standing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: That is correct, there is no PJP uniform. If this is from the period when we already got the green uniforms, but until that time we wore those blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would tell you from other evidence we've had indications that based on the one red ribbon on the left shoulder this -- that's consistent with the order for, I think, the 28th or 29th of July, 1998. Do you know why Salipur would have a green camouflage uniform that early?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the uniform worn by Salipur is not a PJP uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the man on the front row on the left with the headband, can you tell what kind of uniform he's wearing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I cannot see his pants and their colour on the picture before me. The upper part is no uniform, I think it's a civilian T-shirt and a tactical vest of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that you tried to prevent people from wearing non-standard uniforms, but because it was so hot it was difficult. Was there any discipline for people not wearing the standard uniforms in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: It would be a minor or a serious violation of work duty. I don't know whether anyone was processed for that since I don't think there were any flagrant violations of that order and people wearing completely different uniforms. However, there were occasions such as this when people would take photographs after actions while resting and waiting for the trucks that were supposed to take the policemen to the base. Because it was so hot, people were allowed to take off items of clothing and moments like those they were usually taking photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally and your unit, your Belgrade detachment, take part in any anti-terrorist actions in July and August of 1998? I think you've told us about one at least.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see Goran Radosavljevic in the field during that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what his job was in July through October of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I will try to be precise. During the anti-terrorist actions, that is when I did not see him; however, I did see him several times in Kosovo in informal situations. I don't know what he was doing there. However, I did not see him during the anti-terrorist actions. I'm sorry, I forgot what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, if you had seen him in the field in 1998, and I think you've answered it. You were asked a question about whether or not the 122nd Intervention Brigade had any combat vehicles like tanks or artillery, and you said it didn't have any tanks but it had armoured vehicles what you mentioned. In 1998 or in 1999 were you aware of the MUP or the PJP having tanks at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I knew that the MUP or the PJP did not have tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- were there occasions where a tank and a tank team, personnel, were in essence loaned to a MUP unit and travelled around with them during these operations? Were you ever aware of that happening?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that tanks were ever loaned to the police since we didn't know how to operate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you an exhibit that I think you were shown earlier by one of the other Defence lawyers, it's Exhibit P1993. I can hand you a hard copy with help from the usher. This is a meeting dated the 11th of May, 1999, in Pristina at the MUP staff headquarters, and we see several PJP detachment commanders or brigade company commanders that attended. We don't see your name, but if you could turn to page 2 of the B/C/S we'll see Colonel Buha attended this meeting and he's listed as the commander of the 22nd PJP Detachment. You see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In May of 1999, what unit were you a part of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In May 1999 I was in the Pec part of the detachment under the command of Bosko Buha, but in one period of time I -- but in one period of time I -- well, now was this in May, I was resubordinated with two companies to the Podujevo part of the Belgrade detachment during one action, that is to say under Colonel Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what unit designator did that group have? That was just -- that was also part of the 22nd PJP Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: That is part of the 122nd Intervention Brigade, that is the part under paragraph 2 when the deputy commander of the 122nd Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Nikolic, attended the meeting. So it's that part of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's where I got confused, I guess. I think Judge Bonomy asked you about that earlier today. So Buha is the commander of the 22nd Detachment and the 22nd Detachment is a part of the 122nd Brigade, is that right, in May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: That's right, as is written here, the 22nd Detachment of the PJP, the part under the command of Colonel Bosko Buha is one part or the Pec part, if I can call it that, of the 122nd Intervention Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there a name for the Podujevo part of the 122nd?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether there was a numerical designator, but we identified it as the Podujevo part of the Belgrade detachment, or of the 122nd Intervention Brigade, and as the Pec part of that same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, it lists Colonel Dragan Nikolic as the deputy commander of the 122nd Intervention Brigade. Who was the overall commander of the 122nd on 11 May 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Colonel Zivaljevic. At the same time he was the commander of that part, that is to say the Pec part of that brigade, and the commander of the entire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so he would have been Buha's boss, Buha's superior, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next one on your page in B/C/S is the commander of the 23rd PJP Detachment, Colonel Josipovic. Did -- was the 23rd any part of the 122nd Intervention Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Thank you. I want you to go to page 4 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is important to you, Mr. Hannis, and whether the problem is translation, but if you go to page 75, line 17, you would, I think, be excused for thinking that Buha was the commander of the 22nd Detachment, which is the Pec part; and then if you go to 76, 2, you might be excused for thinking that Zivaljevic was the commander of the Pec part. So if you want it to be clear, I can tell you that as far as I can see at the moment it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I may have misheard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, you told us that Colonel Zivaljevic was the overall commander of the 122nd, but I think you told us he was also the commander of another part of the brigade, which part was that? Was that the Podujevo part?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I will be very specific. There is a problem because in this document they didn't state these details very precisely. The commander of the 122nd Intervention Brigade was Colonel Zivaljevic, Dragan. The deputy commander of the 122nd Intervention Brigade was Major or Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Buha. I was one of the assistant commanders. Due to the breadth of the territory that we held in 1999, this detachment was subdivided into two parts, or rather, this brigade was subdivided into two parts: The Pec part and the Podujevo part. I do not know whether in this subdivision every one of these two parts of the detachment got a particular numerical designator. We would recognise each other as the Podujevo and the Pec parts respectively. At the same time the Podujevo part was taken over by the commander of the entire brigade, Colonel Zivaljevic that is; and the Pec part was taken over by his deputy, Bosko Buha, and he was in command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But there was one part of that answer that confused something for me. You're translated as having said that Buha was deputy commander of the brigade, and here it lists Nikolic as the deputy commander of the brigade. Can you explain that for me? I see Buha is listed as a full colonel and Nikolic is listed as a lieutenant-colonel, but I don't know if that makes a difference or not. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I'll try. In the Podujevo part of that unit where Colonel Zivaljevic was, he appointed as his deputy Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Nikolic. This appointment does not mean that he gets a decision of appointment. Decisions of appointment were not distributed in special police units. He was just told so, it was stated to him orally, whereas in the Pec part Bosko Buha appointed orally me as his own deputy. Now, there really is quite a confusion there. I understand you. We are either assistant commanders or deputy commanders, but I think that it's easiest to understand it in the following way. At the moment when these two detachments split up, in the Pec part Commander Zivaljevic, deputy Nikolic, or rather, in the Podujevo part, Commander Zivaljevic, deputy Nikolic; and in the Pec part, Bosko Buha and deputy Vladimir Ilic, or rather, I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But between Nikolic and Buha, who was superior? Is Nikolic deputy of the whole brigade or is he only deputy of the Podujevo part?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: No. He is deputy only for the Podujevo part, and I am deputy only for the Pec part, and Bosko is only the commander of the Pec part. If it would happen that, say, the brigade would get together, then we'd go back to the old system. The commander of the entire brigade is Zivaljevic again, the deputy is Bosko Buha, and we are assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move onto page 4 in the B/C/S and it's page 5 in the English part I want. Mr. Ilic, you'll see there under item number 8 we have the commander of the 35th PJP Detachment, Colonel Prljevic speaking. And the fourth bullet point under him it says: "In the final operations around Cicavica and Bajgora, we worked without technical equipment and support; we had no problems, therefore I can return Srdjan Grekulovic's two tanks, as we do not need them ..." And we see earlier in this document that Srdjan Grekulovic is the commander of the 36th PJP Detachment. What tanks would those be that the 35th PJP Detachment commander has which he can return to Colonel Grekulovic, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't have tanks. I think it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Further down under him, I think -- yeah, it's the big bullet point, the next-to-the-last one under his name. He's talking about: "In final operations, particularly when my unit was being introduced on Jezerce, I had some problems ..." And the next one says: "We had to work on some points again with Sigma and Jastreb ..." Do you know what those are, aren't those some kind of aircraft?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I can't find that part, but I know what it is. Sigma is the call-sign for the 23rd Detachment and Jastreb, those are the sniper shooters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then if we could go -- if you could go to page 5 in the B/C/S, and you'll see it's Colonel Mitrovic from the 37th PJP Detachment speaking. And we'll have to go to the top of page 6 in the English, please. I think you told us you knew Colonel Mitrovic, he was head of the 37th Detachment. I think we had evidence that's from Nis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I personally met him after 2001 when he was transferred to work in the gendarmerie. During the course of the war I had heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: We did not know each other personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go down to the fifth bullet point under his name, he's talking about relations between the SUP and the OUP and actions around Budakovo and Jezerce. You see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the very next one says: "The leadership of Legija in the final operations was felt, particularly when some equipment was used, which helped us a lot." Do you know what he's referring to there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what it was that he meant there. If this is supposed to be a reference to Legija, the commander of the JSO, well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the JSO being involved in any actions in Kosovo in 1998 or in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: In 1998 in June when I was in Decani, we acted in coordination with the JSO in the area of Decani, in an anti-terrorist action in Decani and in the area of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about in 1999, do you know about them being involved in any anti-terrorist or KLA actions in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I think they took part in 1999 as well, but I cannot remember exactly in which actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go to page 6 in your B/C/S copy, and it's on page 8 of the English. And I will tell you that this is General Stevanovic speaking, and actually I'll need to go to near the bottom of the page for you. All the way to the bottom, thank you. It's point number 5 and he's talking about tasks. The first bullet point there says: "Police units are subordinate to the chief of the SUP and PJP detachment and police heads must attend every SUP collegium." Now, did you as deputy to Buha ever attend a SUP collegium in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Buha attended any of those SUP collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, further on at the very bottom of the page the last two points, one says the PJP Detachment must be staffed with officers in exact accordance with establishment. And then it says: "It particularly pertains to the 122nd Intervention Brigade which ought to submit its establishment list with a completely formed PJP detachment by 30 May 1999; nobody is allowed to make changes to this without this detachment commander's approval. At the same time the 121st and 72nd OPJP, PJP detachments, are to be set apart." Can you explain for us what that's about. Do you know what they're talking -- what Stevanovic is talking about there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I can assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if it's an assumption based on some reason or something you personally knew about at the time, then go ahead; if you're just guessing, please don't guess, but if you've got a reasoned basis for it, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If it's speculation I would object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can only determine that when we hear what the witness has to tell us and the basis of his information. Please continue, Mr. Ilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the course of 1998 and 1999 we had frequent shifts of policemen who were sent to Belgrade -- from Belgrade to us. Some were on furlough and others were in Kosovo. Towards the end the situation was that officers from Belgrade would send policemen to the detachment who were not from the PJP because of the security situation in Belgrade. They kept there in order to provide security at places of high risk, like sports games, et cetera, and we were provided with policemen who were not on our lists. What I'm saying I'm saying on the basis of my recollection, and I cannot remember exactly the names of the policemen involved but I think that that problem was the problem on account of which General Stevanovic said this, what is written here, that is to say that policemen cannot be sent who are not within the detachment originally and without the approval of the detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, Mr. Ilic, does that mean that the policemen who were not PJP were being sent to your detachment, they had not been qualified or approved; is that what was happening?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, that was no longer taken into consideration. Those in charge in Belgrade were simply trying to have the right numerical requirements met.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. How far back did that problem go, do you know when it first started?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but for instance as the war was becoming ever more imminent that happened ever more frequently, say from the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us about officers who were assistants to the commander for legal conduct and operation who were sent from the ministry in Belgrade to help dealing with the problems of discipline in connection with violations. Who was the officer sent from Belgrade that dealt with your unit, do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: I recall the deputy head of the department for the control of legality in work, Galovic is his last name, I cannot remember his first name; he's retired now. And in addition to himself he had a few of his own officers but I cannot remember their names because they also came in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned that there were between 50 and 70 policemen from your detachment - or I think later on you explained it was from the whole brigade - who faced disciplinary proceedings as well as criminal proceedings. How do you know about that number, 50 to 70? Did you have a report about it or some document about it or did people talk about it? How do you know that was the number?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: Colonel Zivaljevic told me about that, but the exact figure is in the department for the control of lawfulness in work in -- of the former secretariat of the interior in Belgrade. I think that all these records still exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that those were crimes from the domain of property-related crime, mainly theft, also smuggling of cattle. How many of those 50 to 70 were for something more serious than a disciplinary matter or a property-related crime? Were there any for crimes against life and limb out of those 50 to 70?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC
utterances.text: For us theft was a serious matter too because that did not befit a policeman. That is why disciplinary and criminal reports were filed; however, I do not think that we had any cases pertaining to maltreatment. As far as I know, we did not have such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You referred to smuggling cattle, which is a concept I'm not understanding I don't think. Do you mean rustling or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the crime of smuggling cattle from Kosovo to Serbia. I don't know what the exact wording is for that particular crime, but at any rate it is an incrimination, it is a crime and criminal reports were filed against them. I know that for sure and they were dealt with before a disciplinary court and before a regular court, that is to say a criminal court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't really help me. Are you saying that policemen were taking their own cattle from Kosovo to Serbia and they weren't allowed to or were they stealing cattle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't their cattle. It was the cattle that they found in Kosovo, cattle roaming about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's smuggling got to do with it? Smuggling means you're breaking the rules about crossing the border. Were you not allowed to take cattle from Kosovo to other parts of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could not do that because it wasn't their cattle. They were not the owners of that cattle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stealing cattle, then. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, there was one brief procedural matter I wanted to raise about a witness coming later in the week. I wonder if we could break for the day because I have about 30 minutes more to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we can break at this stage. Mr. Ilic, your evidence is not quite complete and you will have to come back tomorrow to finish it because we have to finish our proceedings for the day at this stage. Between now and resuming your evidence, it's vital that you have no discussion, no communication, with anyone else about any aspect of your evidence or any of the evidence in this case. You can talk about other subjects with whoever you like, but you must not discuss any aspect of the evidence in this case. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and return to resume evidence at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This relates to the third and last witness noticed for this week, Mr. Paponjak. I'm told that we just -- we just received his statement. I had meant to bring this up earlier. We had not yet received his statement. We had a concern about the 48-hour rule. We also had a concern about the vast number of exhibits that were listed with him in the attachment, it's about four or five pages' worth. I don't have the exact count. Earlier in the day the notice -- the information I had was that about 45 of those were untranslated. The explanation we saw in the related motion to add exhibits to the 65 ter list were that the witness had brought these documents with him, but I note that he testified in the Milosevic case and it's my understanding from Ms. Kravetz, who will be handling this witness, that the overwhelming majority of those documents were, indeed, exhibits in the Milosevic case in which he testified in 2005. So we have a concern about that sort of late notice and it puts Ms. Kravetz in a difficult spot to be able to organize all those, and that's what I wanted to bring to your attention. We now have the statement, so that's resolved. I didn't know if it was going to be a new statement or if it was going to be the five days of transcript from Milosevic, but I see we now have a specific statement. But we do have that ongoing concern about the untranslated documents and which of those may be referred to in the statement. That's what it's about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And has Mr. Ivetic not told you which ones will be referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, because I just now saw the statement on the screen. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it was just released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We intervene when necessary and don't intervene when unnecessary, Mr. Hannis. So what is it you're saying we should be doing, apart from worrying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know if they're going to use the five pages worth of exhibits, but our complaint is when it's that substantial amount of material -- and the justification for adding it to the 65 ter list was that this witness just brought them. My position is these are materials they've had for years because the exact same documents were used as exhibits in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying there's an outstanding application in relation to this witness to amend this Rule 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. And have you responded to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, we haven't because we've been trying to sort out during the day which of those indeed are new and which may have been available for some time. And as I said, when I first raised the issue to the court officer this morning we didn't have a statement and so I was concerned about that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds as though your position needs to be firmed up, Mr. Hannis, before we can do anything about it. No doubt that can be done for tomorrow morning by Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And hopefully she'll have a discussion with Mr. Ivetic to clarify anything that's not clear, and then if there's something that we need to adjudicate upon you can raise it with us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we shall adjourn now and resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
